description: We are Pantheon Code. We are curious, creative and passionate about science, technology and understanding our planet. For this challenge, we explore how MODIS and VIIRS satellite data can help us understand fire hotspots and identify patterns. We value teamwork, creativity and learning. We welcome people interested in Earth science, data analysis, visualization, statistics, agriculture, habitats, weather and satellite technology. All skill levels are welcome!
summary:
EmberSpot is a web-app prototype that turns a decade of MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into a burning activity calendar for a selected region. We built it for Cuyo, Argentina, which is one of the most critical regions on our country, and we used NASA FIRMS/LANCE data from 2016 to 2026.
The app shows two linked calendars: the current year, day by day, and a historical reference built from the median of the previous ten years for the same date, colored by relative levels of detected activity. These are the values and their respective colors:
Green: Low (1-17 detections)
Yellow: Moderate (18–34 detections)
Orange: High (35–77 detections)
Red: Very high (78 or more detections)
Grey: No record
As MODIS and VIIRS differ in resolution and sensitivity, their records are not directly comparable. EmberSpot brings both sensors into a single view so fire managers and emergency responders can check whether today looks unusual compared with past years, anticipate critical periods, and focus monitoring. It helps emergency responders, scientists and land managers check whether a period looks unusual, anticipate critical times and focus monitoring. New satellite detections are fetched automatically through an API and added to the app every hour, so the present calendar stays up to date. Next steps include worldwide area selection, Sentinel data and environmental conditions that favor fire spread.
details:
What it does: EmberSpot shows when satellites detected heat across Cuyo, Argentina, and compares the present with the past. The “2026 heat detections” calendar shows each day of the year, and the “Past records, 2016–2025” calendar shows the middle count for the same date among previous years with records. Days are colored from low to very high (1–17, 18–34, 35–77 and 78+ detections), and gray means no record, which does not mean no fire. Selecting a day shows a panel comparing 2026 with the past, showing how many past years have records and each year’s MODIS and VIIRS counts. A filter lets users see all detections or only days found by both satellite systems.

How it works: We downloaded MODIS and VIIRS data and near-real-time detections from NASA FIRMS/LANCE, filtered them to the study region, and summarized them by day. The app computes the historical middle count and color ranges from the distribution of daily counts. A status banner shows the update state of each satellite source.

We also connected the web app to an API that retrieves new near-real-time detections and loads them into the app every hour. Satellites pass over an area only a few times a day and NASA publishes new detections with a delay of up to about three hours, so an hourly refresh means the app picks up new data as soon as it is released, not that detections are continuous.

Benefits and intended impact: Fire managers and emergency responders can quickly see if the current period looks unusual compared with previous years, spot the times of year when detections concentrate, and prepare resources ahead of critical periods. The interface uses simple colors and one screen so non-experts can use it. Because the current calendar updates automatically, responders can check recent activity without manual downloads.

Tools: HTML, CSS, Visual Studio Code JavaScript with a Lucide SVG iconand, Node.js built-in test runner, GeoJSON.io, Git and GitHub, circli, json, docker, docker composed and Railway. Data from NASA FIRMS/LANCE (MODIS Terra-Aqua, VIIRS Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21). IA used. Claude and Codex.

Creativity: Instead of a map of dots, we present fire activity as a calendar (as the challenge itself asks us to do) that answers a practical question: “is this data unusual for this time?” The side-by-side present/past view makes the comparison immediate.

Factors we considered: MODIS and VIIRS have different resolutions, so we had to adapt the data to harmonize them and join them. Also, we had to pass all the information from the past ten years, changing all the hours to UTC and select the ones that were hot spots in Cuyo. We also removed repeated detections at the same location, which mostly captures fixed sources, but may also remove some repeat fires; we list this as a limitation, lthough heat detection is not necessarily a fire. It can be an agricultural burn or a fixed industrial source, and a day without records is not a day without fires, because of overpass times, clouds and smoke. Colors show the number of detections, not fire severity. Past years may have missing records, so the comparison is a rough guide and cannot show whether the number of fires changed. We have to remember that this is a prototype, and we have planned to develop our work in the future.

Future work:

  • Select any area in the world: Let users draw or pick a region and load FIRMS detections for it, so the calendar works anywhere. Cuyo was our prototype, as we are from this region and it is one of the most affected areas in our country with fires.
  • Better harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS: Place both sensors on a common ~1 km grid, keep the maximum fire radiative power per cell and day, and classify days by FRP instead of counts.
  • Sentinel data: Add Sentinel-2 (vegetation condition and burned-area mapping), Sentinel-1 radar (soil moisture and burn mapping) and Sentinel-3 thermal observations as an independent check of detections.
  • Environmental conditions: Add NDVI, land cover, soil moisture (SMAP), precipitation (GPM IMERG), temperature, humidity and wind, to study what promotes ignition and spread, and to separate ignition causes (for example lightning data). Conditions do not tell us what started a fire, but combined with lightning data and local records they can help narrow down likely causes.
  • Alerts and prediction. The hourly refresh already brings in new detections; next we would send notifications (for example by email or messaging) when a new detection appears inside a user’s chosen area, and later test a validated model for periods and zones of higher risk.
  • Validation with local agencies such as provincial fire management services, to adapt the tool to real operations.
  • Add a confidence indicator: Add a level of confidence about how sure is that the fire truly happened or not
